_metadata.independence: I read only u20-blind-input.json; no other file, search, web lookup or API was used.

hints.reason: Rose wreaths exist (funeral flowers), but a wreath does not point at a ghost without a chain of grave-to-haunting reasoning.
Ghosts rise from graves, and a rose laid on a grave is a familiar graveside scene.
Rose scent is immediate; the ghost side relies on the ghost-story trope of an unexplained perfume, which many players will not reach.

best_available.why: The only hint that gives a shared scene (roses on a haunted grave) rather than a one-sided definition.

pairs.pair_note: One solid shared-scene hint; the other two lean almost entirely on ROSE.

hints.reason: Spilling salt is a known superstition, but nothing about spilling points at a ghost.
A salt circle wards off ghosts and spirits in folklore and TV (Supernatural), and seance circles summon them, so the circle links both sides.
Salt thrown over the shoulder is immediate; the ghost side (a presence looking over your shoulder, salt over the shoulder to blind the devil) is recognisable but softer.

best_available.why: Folklore gives a real shared scene: a ring of salt keeps the ghost out.

pairs.pair_note: CIRCLE carries the pair; SHOULDER is a defensible second if a softer ghost route is acceptable.

hints.reason: A shadow follows you everywhere and a ghost follows (haunts) a person; shared verb.
Ghostly figure and shadowy figure are both stock phrases for a half-seen presence.

best_available.why: Both compounds are everyday phrases pointing to the same spooky half-seen shape.

pairs.pair_note: Two clean hints; the pair is easy because the words are already close.

hints.reason: Jaws is the shark film; there is no ghost route at all.
Great white shark on one side, the white sheet ghost on the other; a colour, but anchored in a compound and a stock image.

best_available.why: Great white plus the classic white ghost reaches both words at once.

pairs.pair_note: WHITE is a strong serve; JAWS is pure filler on the ghost side.

hints.reason: Ghosts glide across the floor and snakes glide through grass; shared verb of silent movement.
Ghosts rattle chains and a rattlesnake rattles; both routes are stock.
Snakes shed skin, but shedding has no ghost meaning a player would see.

best_available.why: Chain-rattling ghost and rattlesnake are both instantly recognisable.

pairs.pair_note: Two good verb and compound routes; SHED is one-sided.

hints.reason: Both are standard Halloween decorations and costumes.
The haunted attic and the spider-filled attic are the same dusty room.
Spiders spin cobwebs, and cobwebs dress every haunted house a ghost lives in.

best_available.why: Broadest shared scene with both words equally present.

pairs.pair_note: All three hints work; a strong pair.

hints.reason: A spring feeds a well (wellspring); the ghost in the well is a known horror image (The Ring) but needs that reference.
Ghosts rise from the grave; water rises from a spring and things spring up, but the spring side is diffuse.
Holy Ghost is a fixed phrase and holy springs or sacred wells are a familiar idea; both are compounds.

best_available.why: Holy Ghost is unmistakable and holy spring is a real, recognisable phrase.

pairs.pair_note: A hard pair; HOLY is the only hint that reaches both words through ordinary phrases.

hints.reason: A ghost is a dead person and a dead star is an everyday astronomy phrase.
Patrick Swayze is the star of the film Ghost; a proper name used as a hint.

best_available.why: Broadest shared property; works without any pop-culture knowledge.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; SWAYZE is clever but skews to older players.

hints.reason: Phantom is a straight synonym for ghost; the phantom train is a real trope but weaker than ghost train itself.
The Polar Express is a train; the hobo ghost on its roof is too obscure to count as a ghost route.
The Hogwarts Express is a train and Hogwarts is full of ghosts (Nearly Headless Nick); one world, both words.

best_available.why: A single famous setting that contains both a train and ghosts.

pairs.pair_note: HOGWARTS is the serve; PHANTOM gives away the ghost side.

hints.reason: Ghost ship is a fixed phrase and ships sail on water.
Ghosts moan; the water side exists only via Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, which is an explanation not a connection.
Drowning happens in water and the drowned ghost is a standard ghost-story figure.

best_available.why: Ghost ship is the cleanest compound bridging both words.

pairs.pair_note: Two good hints; MOANING fails on the water side.

hints.reason: Haunted is essentially the ghost's own adjective; witches appear in haunted houses only as general spookiness.
Ghost and witch are the two classic Halloween costumes.
Hocus Pocus is the witch film and hocus pocus is witchcraft; the ghost in that film (Binx's spirit) is a detail, not a route most players hold.

best_available.why: Equal, obvious footing for both words.

pairs.pair_note: HALLOWEEN is the natural serve; the other two tilt toward one side each.

hints.reason: In Game of Thrones, Ghost is Jon Snow's direwolf, so one name literally covers both words for anyone who knows the show.
Wolves howl at the moon and ghosts howl through haunted halls; shared sound verb.
The foggy moor hosts both ghosts (Wuthering Heights) and wolf-like hounds (Baskervilles), but neither link is strong on its own.

best_available.why: Broad shared verb that needs no franchise knowledge.

pairs.pair_note: HOWL is universal; THRONES is a sharp pass for fans and a blank for others.

hints.reason: Gold leaf is a compound; gilding on glass is a craft detail players will not reach from LEAF.
A gold-rimmed glass is a single familiar object.
Goblets are made of glass or of gold; both are stock images.

best_available.why: Both materials are classic goblet materials.

pairs.pair_note: Two good object hints; LEAF is one-sided.

hints.reason: Broken glass and broken heart are both everyday phrases.
Glass shatters and hearts are shattered; same route as BROKEN with a stronger verb.
Fragile is the stock property of glass and of a tender heart.

best_available.why: The most familiar phrase on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: All three pass; a very natural pair.

hints.reason: Honey is amber-coloured and amber glass is a standard bottle colour; a shared property, like SWEET for APPLE+HONEY.
A honey jar is a glass jar; one object.

best_available.why: The glass honey jar is literally both words in one object.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass.

hints.reason: Glass figurines are a classic ornament and horses are a classic figurine subject.
A horse-drawn carriage on one side and Cinderella's glass carriage on the other.
The Glass Menagerie is a famous play of glass animals, but its signature animal is a unicorn and the horse side is only generic.

best_available.why: Glass horse figurines are a recognisable single object.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; MENAGERIE needs the play and still only half-reaches horse.

hints.reason: Glass ceiling is a stock phrase; there is no familiar iron ceiling.
Greenhouses are glass; the Victorian iron-and-glass frame is real but not what most players picture.
An old lantern is iron frame with glass panes; one familiar object.

best_available.why: The only hint where both materials are visible in the same object.

pairs.pair_note: LANTERN carries the pair; CEILING is one-sided filler.

hints.reason: Glass case is immediate; a key case is not a phrase players hold.
Glass cabinets and locked key cabinets (or the cabinet key) both land.

best_available.why: A glass-fronted cabinet that locks with a key is a single scene.

pairs.pair_note: CABINET works; CASE is one-sided.

hints.reason: King Arthur is obvious; the glass side (Glastonbury as the Isle of Glass) is scholarly trivia.
A king drinks from a goblet and goblets are made of glass.
Kings live in castles; the glass castle (memoir title, fairy-tale image) is a thinner phrase.

best_available.why: Clean shared object.

pairs.pair_note: GOBLET is the serve; ARTHUR is invented on the glass side.

hints.reason: A knight's helmet visor is immediate; a glass visor (motorcycle or space helmet) is a loose association.
Stained glass is a compound and knights are a common stained-glass subject, but the knight side depends on picturing a church window.

best_available.why: A stained-glass knight is a real image players may see once prompted; VISOR barely reaches glass.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; both hints are half-connections.

hints.reason: A glass prism splits light; one object, both words.
A light bulb is a glass bulb.
Windows are glass and let in light.

best_available.why: Most everyday object that is both.

pairs.pair_note: All pass.

hints.reason: Lions live at the zoo; the glass of the enclosure is there but secondary.
The Glass Menagerie gives the glass side and a menagerie is a collection of exotic beasts led by lions; both sides are real but literary.

best_available.why: The only hint with a genuine route to both words, though it rewards readers.

pairs.pair_note: Thin pair; MENAGERIE passes narrowly and ZOO is mostly lion.

hints.reason: Full moon and a full glass are both everyday phrases.
A telescope's glass lenses point at the moon; one scene.
Lenses are glass; the moon arrives only via the implied telescope.

best_available.why: Two stock phrases with equal weight.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; LENS is a weaker form of TELESCOPE.

hints.reason: Mouse pad is a compound; nothing links a pad to glass.
The glass slipper and the helpful mice are both central to Cinderella.

best_available.why: One story with both words as famous elements.

pairs.pair_note: CINDERELLA is strong; PAD is one-sided.

hints.reason: Rule failure: the hint contains the target NIGHT, even though a nightcap is a glass of something at night.
A glass of wine is immediate; wine at night is only a loose evening association.
A glass lantern is lit at night; one scene.

best_available.why: Clean object-and-scene route to both words.

pairs.pair_note: LANTERN is the serve; NIGHTCAP must be removed as a contains_target failure.

hints.reason: An aquarium is a glass tank holding ocean life.
Sea glass is a real compound, but sea is a near-synonym that hands over the ocean side.
A glass bottle with a message in it floats across the ocean.

best_available.why: Both words are present in the one object.

pairs.pair_note: Two clean passes; SEA is a judgement call on the synonym rule.

hints.reason: Pirates drink rum and rum comes in a glass.
Rule failure: the hint contains the target GLASS, though the pirate spyglass is otherwise a perfect bridge.
Glass eye and the pirate's eye patch are both stock images.
Glass bottles of rum and ships in bottles belong to the pirate world.

best_available.why: Glass eye and pirate eye are each a two-word phrase a player sees at once.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes; SPYGLASS must be dropped for containing the target.

hints.reason: Glass slipper is Cinderella's, and the story's royal is a prince, not a queen.
Mirrors are glass and the evil queen asks 'mirror, mirror' in Snow White.

best_available.why: Snow White gives a shared scene on the owner's POISON calibration model.

pairs.pair_note: MIRROR is strong; SLIPPER misses the queen.

hints.reason: Glasses clink in a toast; a struck glass rings, but ring-as-sound is a secondary reading of the target.
Crystal glassware and a crystal ring are both familiar objects.
Raising a glass is the toast; the ring only arrives via an implied wedding.

best_available.why: A material both objects are commonly made of.

pairs.pair_note: CRYSTAL is the only hint that reaches the ring directly.

hints.reason: Glass dome is a compound; the retro robot's glass dome head is a recognisable but dated image.
Screens are glass; a robot with a screen face is plausible but not a fixed association.

best_available.why: The glass-domed robot head is a single image players may recall; SCREEN is more diffuse.

pairs.pair_note: No PASS; both hints reach robot only through a specific mental picture.

hints.reason: Glass shatters, and a rock through a window is the thing that shatters it, but rock is the agent rather than the subject.
Glass houses is immediate; the rock side depends on the proverb's thrown stones.
Obsidian is volcanic glass and a rock; one word is literally both.

best_available.why: A rock that is glass; exact on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: OBSIDIAN is the serve; the other two circle the same glass-house-and-stone image.

hints.reason: Beauty and the Beast's enchanted rose sits under a glass bell jar; one famous scene.
Stained glass is immediate; the rose window of a cathedral is real but a specialist term.
Roses stand in a glass vase.

best_available.why: Everyday object that holds both words.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; STAINED needs the rose-window term.

hints.reason: A salted rim on a cocktail glass is one image.
A salt shaker is a glass shaker.
The margarita glass with its salt rim carries both words.

best_available.why: Most direct shared image.

pairs.pair_note: All pass.

hints.reason: Shadows are dark and dark (tinted) glass is a familiar phrase; a shared property on the SWEET model.
Smoked glass is a compound; smoke is not shadow.
Tinted glass is immediate and there is no shadow route.

best_available.why: The only hint that touches shadow at all.

pairs.pair_note: A hard pair; DARK passes narrowly as a shared property, the rest are glass-only.

hints.reason: Shark cage diving is immediate; the cage is steel and no glass cage phrase is familiar.
The aquarium glass tunnel with sharks swimming overhead is one scene.
Shark tank is a fixed phrase and tanks are glass.

best_available.why: Shark tank plus glass tank, both stock phrases.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; CAGE misses glass.

hints.reason: The glass lizard is a real legless lizard and lizards are snake kin, but neither route is strong for a general player.
A pet snake lives in a glass terrarium.
Snake tank and glass tank; same object as TERRARIUM in plainer words.

best_available.why: Specific to reptiles and unmistakably glass.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; LIZARD is too oblique.

hints.reason: Trapping a spider under a glass jar is a familiar household scene.
Windows are glass and spiders spin webs in window corners.
Glass cracks, and a spider crack is the web-shaped pattern, but the spider link rides on that one phrase.

best_available.why: Spider under a glass is the shared scene.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; CRACK is a fair stretch via the web-shaped crack.

hints.reason: Greenhouses are glass; spring planting links the season only loosely.
A glass of water and spring water are both everyday phrases.
Glass bottle is immediate; spring arrives only as the bottled spring water inside.

best_available.why: Two stock phrases that meet in a glass of spring water.

pairs.pair_note: WATER is the serve; the other two orbit it.

hints.reason: Glass ornaments and the star ornament on a Christmas tree.
Stars twinkle; glass sparkles rather than twinkles, so the glass side is approximate.
Glass lenses pointed at the stars.

best_available.why: Both words live in the same instrument and its use.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; TWINKLE leans on star.

hints.reason: Train station is immediate; the glass roof of a grand station is a secondary image.
Dining car is a train compound; dining glassware is only a loose association.
Train windows are glass; looking out of one is a shared scene.

best_available.why: The train window is a single everyday object made of glass.

pairs.pair_note: WINDOW carries the pair; the other two are train-first.
